South Carolina. One of the original thirteen colonies, South Carolina played a pivotal role in American history as a center of plantation slavery and a bastion of southern secession. Wealthy planter elites dominated the colony and state, building vast rice and cotton fortunes on enslaved African labor. Established as a British colony in 1670, Charleston became a major Atlantic port for the slave trade and colonial commerce. The state developed an extreme concentration of wealth and enslaved people. By 1800, the majority of South Carolina's population was enslaved Africans and African Americans, creating a slave-majority society. Rice plantations in the coastal lowcountry generated enormous wealth through slave labor, making slaveholders a planter aristocracy with outsized political influence over colonial and later state affairs. South Carolina was home to the Nullification Crisis from 1828 to 1833, when the state asserted that states could reject federal tariffs they deemed unconstitutional, threatening national unity. The state produced intellectual defenders of slavery, including John C. Calhoun, whose theories of states' rights and minority protection shaped Southern ideology and secession movements. South Carolina became the first state to secede from the Union in December 1860 after Abraham Lincoln's election, directly triggering the American Civil War. Fort Sumter, where Confederate forces fired the first shots of the Civil War in April 1861, stands in Charleston Harbor as a symbol of the conflict's origin. The state also produced Robert Smalls, an enslaved riverboat pilot who boldly seized a Confederate vessel and escaped to the North, later serving in Congress during Reconstruction as a champion of freedom.
